title.official: Court appointment in absence of self-appointment

operative_text.controlling:
2.15(1)  If an individual or estate who is required to have a
litigation representative under rule 2.11 does not have one, an
interested person may, or if there is no interested person, a party
adverse in interest must, apply to the Court for directions about the
appointment of a litigation representative for that individual or
estate.
(2)  On an application under subrule (1), the Court may appoint a
person as litigation representative.

BOOK_A.title: Court Appointment in Absence of Self-appointment
BOOK_A.commentary:
Court appointment of an administrator ad litem is not a nullity, and is valid until set aside, and
so a suit by him is not a nullity and a later-appointed administrator can be substituted.⁵
This Rule creates a duty on the opponent to apply for a litigation representative.⁶
Judges’ inherent powers do not let them appropriate public funds, even to pay an amicus
curiae or other ofﬁcer whom the court has appointed. Only legislatures or Parliament can
authorize spending public funds, and allocation of resources involves policy issues.⁷
A court-appointed representative for a minor gave notice that she no longer wanted to act, yet
continued to take active steps, including instructing her counsel to conduct a JDR about liability.
Quite some time later (without advance notice) she discontinued her own claim. She was held
liable to pay party-party costs up to the date of the discontinuance.⁸

Bonora 195, 2013 ABQB 119 at para. 23 (Alta. Q.B.).
